pages.text: For over 30 years, peregrine falcons have returned to a building at 367 Collins Street in Melbourne. They come here to have babies. A camera shows the birds 24–7. People love to watch the falcons on the internet. These birds are very fast. They can fly at speeds over 320 kilometers per hour. They are the fastest animals on earth.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Peregrine falcon  Falco peregrinus  in flight, Cape Baily, Kamay Botany Bay NSW Jun 2022

pages.text: Since 1991, people have seen them on the roof of this building. It is the only place in the city center where they nest. Fans call the male bird M24 and the female bird F24. Watching them can be exciting. Sometimes the birds make the people nervous. One person said M24 was late one day.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Peregrine Falcon, submelanogenys subspecies, Herdsman Lake near Perth, Western Austraila

pages.text: Another person said it is amazing how the birds know how to be parents. They know how to turn their eggs to keep them safe. The building has a camera on YouTube. Over 30,000 people follow the channel. Many people watch the birds every day. They like to see the chicks grow and learn to fly.
It helps people feel close to nature.

pages.text: For over 30 years, a pair of peregrine falcons has returned to a building at 367 Collins Street in Melbourne, Australia, to breed. This site has become a digital sensation, with a webcam providing 24–7 footage of the birds as they nest, lay eggs, and raise their chicks.

pages.text: These annual visitors have developed a dedicated fan base who eagerly await their arrival each year. Peregrine falcons are renowned as the fastest animals on earth, capable of flying at speeds exceeding 320 kilometers per hour. Since 1991, the rooftop of 367 Collins Street has served as the only known nesting site within Melbourne’s central business district.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Peregrine Falcon, submelanogenys subspecies, Herdsman Lake near Perth, Western Austraila

pages.text: The building plays a vital role in the survival of these rare, territorial birds. Social media followers have nicknamed the pair M24 and F24. Watching the livestream can be a tense experience for fans. One observer, Kirsty Greenwood, noted her anxiety when M24 failed to appear on time, while others marvel at the birds' instinctive parenting skills.

Fans are particularly fascinated by how the falcons instinctively rotate their eggs to ensure proper development. The YouTube channel now boasts over 30,000 subscribers. Whether they are watching the eggs hatch or the chicks take their first flight, the online community remains deeply engaged. As one observer noted, the project allows people to feel connected to nature, even from afar.

pages.text: The rooftop of 367 Collins Street in Melbourne has become an unlikely hub for wildlife enthusiasts. For over 30 years, peregrine falcons have utilized this urban structure as a breeding ground, a phenomenon now broadcast globally via a 24–7 webcam.

pages.text: This digital window into the lives of these raptors—the fastest animals on earth, capable of exceeding 320 kilometers per hour—has cultivated a significant following. Since 1991, the building has hosted these birds, serving as the sole known nesting site within the city’s central business district. The site is critical for the conservation of these fiercely territorial creatures.

pages.text: The public’s fascination is evident in the shorthand adopted by social media users, who refer to the current pair as M24 and F24. The livestream experience is often described as a stressful pastime, with viewers expressing genuine anxiety during shifts in the birds' attendance patterns. Observers frequently comment on the hard-wired, instinctive nature of the falcons' parenting.

The meticulous care taken to rotate eggs to ensure the embryo receives adequate albumen is a source of constant wonder for the audience. While the specific individuals may change—as noted in 2024 when a new female arrived—the public interest remains steadfast.

With over 30,000 subscribers, the YouTube channel provides a rare, intimate look at the lifecycle of these birds, from the initial egg-laying to the eventual fledgling flight. This project highlights a profound human desire to remain connected to the natural world, even within the confines of a modern metropolis.
